2. Is NVIDIA Power Unlock expected to work on this specific Victus configuration?

5. What diagnostic information or controlled tests would you need from me to validate the hardware safely?

My objective is to determine whether this laptop can safely sustain a small increase above its observed 50 W GPU limit, with measurable performance improvements and no firmware modification.

I can provide the OmenCore diagnostic export and additional hardware information. I'm happy to run read-only diagnostics or follow a test procedure you recommend.

title: [8E35] HP Omen 16 (2025) - SMU Table Unknown, Direct EC Blocked & WMI Fan Latency (UI Freeze)
body: Hi, I am using the new HP OMEN 16-ap0xxx (2025) with Ryzen 9 8940HX (Product ID: 8E35). I have been testing OmenCore v4.4.1 and I would like to report two technical issues to help with the verification of this model: 1. SMU Power Table & Tuning Issue: The app reports: "This CPU's SMU power table layout has not been identified". Because of this, AMD Power Limits (STAPM/Tctl) and Curve Optimizer settings do not apply. Even though PawnIO is installed, "Confirmed" values stay at 0 mV. It seems the SMU layout for the 8940HX (2025) is not yet mapped in the database. 2. Fan Latency & WMI Fallback: Since the profile is currently "Inferred/Unverified", the app defaults to WMI BIOS fallback for fan control. This creates a significant latency (~7 seconds). When the CPU temperature spikes (e.g., during a screenshot or alt-tab) to 86°C for a second, the fan response is delayed. By the time the fans reach 4800 RPM, the CPU has already cooled down, but the EC often gets stuck in a high-RPM failsafe mode. I am willing to provide logs or run SmuProbe commands to help you identify the power tables and verify Direct EC access for the 8E35 board. As seen in the attached Model Capabilities screenshot, Direct EC writes are completely disabled on my 8E35 board. PawnIO-Only mode does not work at all, leaving me completely stuck with the 7-second WMI fallback latency. P.S: While the WMI latency is occurring, the entire OmenCore UI freezes and stutters heavily. It seems the WMI fallback calls are blocking the main UI thread during these 7-second delays. body: My custom fan curve was keeping the fans at ~2000rpm while the CPU hit 100°C. Found the cause: the daemon's CPU temp has been exactly 20°C since boot. It never changes, not once in the whole journal: ``` [FanCurve] Temp: 54°C (CPU: 20°C, GPU: 54°C) -> Fan: 38% [FanCurve] Temp: 45°C (CPU: 20°C, GPU: 45°C) -> Fan: 28% [FanCurve] Temp: 51°C (CPU: 20°C, GPU: 51°C) -> Fan: 32% ``` That 20°C is acpitz_1, a dead thermal zone on this laptop that sits at exactly +20.0°C forever. The real CPU temp is k10temp. I ran sensors right when the daemon logged those lines: ``` acpitz_1 +20.0°C <- what omencore reports as CPU k10temp +56.4°C <- Tctl, real CPU temp acpitz_0 +56.0°C <- also tracks the CPU acpitz_2 -273.2°C <- broken ``` So the curve only ever sees the GPU temp. In btop the 7940HS was at 99°C, throttled to ~2.7GHz, while fan1 sat at 2000rpm (36%) and PWM duty was 33%. The 95°C thermal emergency never fired either, it uses the same value. There's also no config option to override the temp source as far as I can tell. Details: OMEN 16-xf0xxx, board 8BCA, Ryzen 9 7940HS, Pop!_OS 24.04, kernel 7.1.5-76070105, omencore-cli 4.4.0, access method hp-wmi-hwmon. title: OMEN MAX 16-ak0xxx (board 8D87): Feature request: automatic software fan curves when BIOS Auto under-cools in Performance mode
body:
# Feature request: automatic software fan curves when BIOS Auto under-cools in Performance mode

## TL;DR

- On an HP OMEN MAX 16-ak0xxx (`8D87`, BIOS `F.07`), Linux Performance mode
  applies the expected power limits, including approximately 175 W dGPU power,
  but firmware Auto stops near 3,400/3,600 RPM and allows the CPU to reach
  92–99 C.
- HP OMEN Gaming Hub does more than select the Performance profile: while the
  machine is active, its Auto mode runs a userspace EWMA controller, evaluates
  separate CPU/GPU/IR curves, selects the highest request, maps it through the
  firmware fan table, and writes discrete fan levels through HP WMI.
- The exact factory Performance curves and the complete 128-byte `0x2f` fan
  mapping response have been extracted for this machine.
- Gaming Hub's IR input was identified as HP WMI `0x23`, sensor index `0`;
  neither Linux `acpitz` zone exposes the same reading on `8D87`.
- A standalone Linux prototype reproduced the factory curve through `hp-wmi`:
  fan speed increased to about 4,600/4,800 RPM and sustained CPU temperature
  stabilized around 85.5 C instead of the firmware-Auto result.
- Proposal: add an opt-in, safety-gated automatic curve controller to OmenCore,
  initially for explicitly validated systems.

## System and Linux reproduction

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Product | HP OMEN MAX Gaming Laptop 16-ak0xxx |
| Board / BIOS | `8D87` / `F.07` |
| Distribution / kernel | Arch Linux (Omarchy) / `7.1.9-arch1-2` |
| Platform profile | `performance` |
| Firmware fan mode | `pwm1_enable=2` (Auto) |
| Observed Auto ceiling | 3,400/3,600 RPM |
| Hardware maximum | approximately 6,000 RPM, verified with manual control |

Reproduction:

1. Select `performance` and verify `/sys/firmware/acpi/platform_profile`.
2. Leave `pwm1_enable=2`.
3. Apply a sustained CPU workload and record temperatures, PWM state, and RPM.

Representative stable samples:

```csv
elapsed_s,profile,cpu_c,gpu_c,acpi_c,fan1_rpm,fan2_rpm,pwm_enable,pwm_percent
0,performance,91.1,49,90.0,3400,3600,2,56.5
4,performance,91.5,50,90.0,3400,3600,2,56.5
8,performance,91.8,50,90.0,3400,3600,2,56.5
11,performance,92.0,50,90.0,3400,3600,2,56.5
```

The logger stopped at its 92 C safety threshold while the workload continued.
All 11 samples in the 90–94 C bin were exactly 3,400/3,600 RPM; another
60-second capture showed the same ceiling. The profile was active, and a
separate power-instrumented GPU test later recorded 174.6 W. The problem is
therefore not profile application or inability to command the fans: it is the
missing automatic software policy used by HP on Windows.

## What Gaming Hub does

The installed Windows package was
`AD2F1837.OMENCommandCenter 1101.2608.1.0 x64`. Its managed assemblies were
decompiled with ILSpyCmd 9.1; relevant code is in `PerformanceControl.dll`,
`HP.Omen.PerformanceControlModule.dll`,
`HP.Omen.Background.PerformanceControl.dll`, and
`HP.Omen.Core.Model.Device.dll`.

### Auto uses a userspace controller

`FanHandler.GetFanSetScheme` selects `EWMA_ALGO` even for Auto while the system
is not idle:

```csharp
case ThermalControl.Auto:
    if (!isIdle)
        return FanSetScheme.EWMA_ALGO;
    return FanSetScheme.IDLE_AUTO;
```

It evaluates separate inputs and takes their maximum:

```csharp
int cpu = GetFanTuning(cpuAdvanced, TuningDevice.Cpu);
int gpu = GetFanTuning(gpuAdvanced, TuningDevice.Gpu);
int ir  = GetFanTuning(irAdvanced,  TuningDevice.Ir);
target = Enumerable.Max(new int[3] { ir, cpu, gpu });
```

The inputs are EWMA-smoothed CPU, GPU, and IR/chassis temperatures. Rise and
fall coefficients are independent. CPU/GPU curves have separate high/low
thresholds; older tables without low thresholds use midpoints when decreasing.
The background loop samples every second, recalculates on an approximately
five-second cadence, and avoids redundant writes.

The selected CPU level is mapped to the other physical fans rather than copied
unchanged:

```csharp
List<int> sameLevelFans = SwFanControlTable.GetSameLevelFans(cpuFanSpeed);
if (sameLevelFans.Count > 1 && sameLevelFans[1] >= 0)
    gpuFanSpeed = sameLevelFans[1];
```

Gaming Hub's logs confirm the relevant state on this machine:

```text
8D87::ThisSystemID
IsSwFanControlSupport = True
GetThermalPolicyVersion = V1
enter GetSwFanControlTable()
leave GetSwFanControlTable(), rawTable is not null
FanType = Cpu
FanType = Gpu
Is3FanNb = False
ThermalMode = Auto
```

### IR sensor source on `8D87`

The device library reads four temperatures through HP WMI command group
`0x20008`, query `0x23`; the first input byte selects the sensor:

```csharp
public static int GetIRSensorValue() {
    return ChangeIrSensorToBoard ? GetSensorValue(1) : GetSensorValue(0);
}

private static int GetSensorValue(byte index) {
    byte[] input = { index, 0, 0, 0 };
    return _omenHsaClient.BiosWmiCmd_GetSync(131080, 35,
        input, input.Length, 4)[0];
}
```

The indices are `0 = IR`, `1 = Ambient`, `2 = PCH`, and `3 = VR`. Gaming Hub's
log for this machine explicitly says `ChangeIrSensorToBoard = False`, so its IR
curve uses index `0`.

A read-only Linux probe sampled the same WMI query alongside both ACPI thermal
zones during a two-minute 50% CPU load. WMI IR changed only `37 -> 39 C`, while
`thermal_zone0` changed `44 -> 66 C` and `thermal_zone1` changed `41 -> 49 C`.
Neither Linux `acpitz` zone is the IR value exposed to Gaming Hub. Zone 1 tracked
the WMI Ambient reading more closely, but this run does not establish that they
are the same firmware source.

## Exact factory Performance curve

Gaming Hub repeatedly selected this embedded configuration:

```text
LoadInitialConfig: Postfix = Vibrance_STX_N22X9
Load resource settings: HP.Omen.Core.Common.PowerControl.JSON.Vibrance_STX_N22X9.json
LoadResourceSettings: Resource version: 20250930
LoadInitialConfig: latestConfigName = Resource
NvGpuModel = NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 Laptop GPU
```

No Local or External configuration was selected. The matching resource was
extracted from `HP.Omen.Core.Common.dll`; decompiled mode-selection code assigns
its `SwFanControlCustomPerformance.FanTable` and coefficients in Performance.

| Sensor | Rising temperatures (C) | Falling temperatures (C) | Fan levels |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU | 60,64,68,71,74,76,78,80,82,83,84,85 | 56,60,64,67,70,72,74,76,78,79,80,81 | 19,20,21,22,23,25,28,31,34,37,43,47 |
| GPU | 57,60,63,66,69,71,73,75,77,78,79,80 | 53,55,58,61,64,67,69,71,73,75,76,77 | 19,20,21,22,23,25,28,31,34,37,43,47 |
| IR | 42,44,46,48,50,52,54,56,58,60,62,64 | not provided | 19,20,21,22,23,25,28,31,34,37,43,47 |

`Lamda_Increase = 0.1`; `Lamda_Decrease = 0.05`. Normal Performance tops out
at level `47`; the separate Unleashed table reaches `60`. A logged local
`CustomFanCurve` (`50..90 C`, levels `20..36`) had `IsEnabled=false` and was not
the source of this behavior.

## HP WMI interface and captured fan mapping

Gaming Hub uses group `131080` / `0x20008` (`HPWMI_GM`):

| Purpose | Command | Direction |
|---|---:|---|
| Fan types/capabilities | `0x2c` | Get |
| Current levels | `0x2d` | Get |
| Software fan levels | `0x2e` | Set |
| Fan mapping table | `0x2f` | Get |
| Thermal/fan mode | `0x1a` | Set |

For `0x2e`, bytes 0 and 1 contain CPU and mapped GPU levels; byte 2 is the
optional third fan and the remainder is zero-filled:

```csharp
data[0] = Convert.ToByte(cpuFanLevel);
data[1] = Convert.ToByte(gpuFanLevel);
if (Is3FanNb)
    data[2] = Convert.ToByte(fan3);
```

`0x2d` returns current non-zero levels. `0x2c` identifies fan types in the low
and high nibbles of its first four bytes and capability flags in byte 8. For
thermal-policy V1, Gaming Hub maps Default/Eco to L2, Performance to L7, and
Cool to L4, then sends `0x1a`; observed L7 is `0x31`. Setting this mode alone
does not start the EWMA loop.

### Exact `0x2f` response from this BIOS

Both Gaming Hub and Linux parse byte 0 as fan count, leave byte 1 unspecified,
then read records containing one level per fan plus a noise/dB index until an
all-zero record. Linux 7.1 independently defines the same two-fan layout.

An eBPF probe captured the complete response while `hp_wmi` initialized. The
ACPI object was 136 bytes: an eight-byte HP response header followed by the
requested 128-byte payload.

```text
00000000  02 3c 13 15 17 14 16 19 16 17 1c 18 1a 1f 1c 1e
00000010  23 1e 20 25 22 24 28 24 26 2a 25 27 2b 2b 2d 2e
00000020  2f 31 30 32 34 32 35 37 33 38 3a 34 3c 3a 35 00
00000030  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
00000040  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
00000050  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
00000060  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
00000070  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
```

SHA-256:
`c9770ef1ffdaa25b7ef8aaa8c42757dbdff1aee07e22227e035e6d1c901a0e2f`.
Header byte 0 is `2`; byte 1 is `0x3c` (60), but neither parser assigns it a
meaning. The 15 records beginning at byte 2 are:

| CPU | GPU | Noise/dB | CPU | GPU | Noise/dB |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 19 | 21 | 23 | 37 | 39 | 43 |
| 20 | 22 | 25 | 43 | 45 | 46 |
| 22 | 23 | 28 | 47 | 49 | 48 |
| 24 | 26 | 31 | 50 | 52 | 50 |
| 28 | 30 | 35 | 53 | 55 | 51 |
| 30 | 32 | 37 | 56 | 58 | 52 |
| 34 | 36 | 40 | 60 | 58 | 53 |
| 36 | 38 | 42 |  |  |  |

The terminator begins at offset `0x2f`; bytes through 127 are zero. The table
proves that CPU and GPU levels are not interchangeable—for example, CPU `47`
maps to GPU `49`, while CPU `60` maps to GPU `58`.

## Standalone Linux prototype

An independent Python prototype uses only the `hp-wmi` hwmon ABI; it neither
calls nor links to OmenCore. It implements:

- the extracted CPU/GPU/IR factory tables and asymmetric coefficients;
- maximum-of-available-sensors selection;
- raw temperature for immediate increases and EWMA/high-low hysteresis for
  decreases;
- configurable TOML curves, rate limits, profile gating, CSV telemetry, and
  NVIDIA power sampling;
- a raw 92 C emergency override to 100%;
- restoration of firmware Auto on exit, signal, profile change, or sensor
  failure.

The Linux `acpitz` sensors remain disabled by default: a direct WMI comparison
confirmed that neither is Gaming Hub's IR input on `8D87`.

### Actuator and controller-development tests

A bounded 60% test confirmed intermediate control and physical ramp time:

```text
elapsed   PWM feedback       fan 1 / fan 2
0 s         0 (0.0%)             0 /    0 RPM
3 s        42 (16.5%)         1000 / 1000 RPM
6 s        97 (38.0%)         2300 / 2400 RPM
9 s       136 (53.3%)         3200 / 3400 RPM
10 s      153 (60.0%)         3600 / 3700 RPM
11–15 s   153 (60.0%)         3600 / 3800 RPM
```

Auto was restored successfully. Five early CPU-only runs then identified two
timing requirements: EWMA alone lagged a raw rise from 74.0 to 93.8 C by about
two seconds, and a 65 C activation threshold started the fans too late. The
final logic uses the higher of raw/EWMA for increases, allows rising updates
every second, retains EWMA for decreases, and activates at 60 C.

| Run | Condition | Peak CPU | Sustained CPU | Result |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | EWMA-only rise | 99.4 C | 90–91 C | Exposed filtered-rise latency. |
| 2 | Profile toggled during load | 100.0 C | 90–92 C | Not comparable; fans began at 0 RPM. |
| 3 | Raw rise, activation at 65 C | 99.8 C | 90–91 C | Motivated earlier pre-spin. |
| 4 | Activation at 60 C | 97.5 C | 89–90 C | Removed 99 C samples. |
| 5 | Repeat without reapplying Performance | 97.8 C | about 89 C | Confirmed profile persistence after Auto restoration. |

Comparable runs used intermediate speeds, reached about
6,000/5,800–6,000 RPM when emergency was required, and restored Auto.

### Factory-curve validation

The final 175-second CPU workload used the exact factory Performance tables.
The ACPI proxy selected level 47 first, but CPU independently reached it at
85 C:

```text
elapsed   raw CPU   controller   request          fan 1 / fan 2
11.0 s     60.1 C   ACPI proxy    85 (33.3%)          0 /    0 RPM
14.3 s     79.0 C   CPU          119 (46.7%)       1000 / 1200 RPM
16.5 s     83.0 C   CPU          157 (61.6%)       2000 / 2000 RPM
18.7 s     83.9 C   ACPI proxy   200 (78.4%)       2700 / 2800 RPM
28.5 s     85.0 C   CPU          200 (78.4%)       4600 / 4800 RPM
```

PWM `200` represents factory level `47/60`; steady readback was `195`, likely
EC/driver quantization. CPU remained at 85.5–85.6 C, versus 92–99 C and
3,400/3,600 RPM in firmware Auto. Emergency was not needed, every sample
remained in `performance`, cooldown used intermediate levels, and Auto was
restored.

A clean CPU-only repeat excluded GPU/ACPI, reached 86.4 C and 4,600/4,800 RPM,
and selected CPU for all 202 controlled samples. A normal CPU+GPU-sensor repeat
reached 87.2/55 C and selected CPU for all 148 controlled samples. Neither run
entered emergency; both restored Auto.

### GPU and combined validation

In a simultaneous CPU/CUDA test with ACPI disabled, GPU initially won at 61 C.
CPU then crossed the independent safety threshold:

```text
elapsed   state       CPU/GPU       request       fan 1 / fan 2
47.9 s    manual      60.5/61 C      33.3%             0 /    0 RPM
63.1 s    manual      91.5/57 C      78.4%          3400 / 3600 RPM
64.3 s    emergency   92.4/57 C     100.0%          3800 / 4000 RPM
74.5 s    emergency   95.8/65 C     100.0%          6000 / 5800 RPM
88.0 s    emergency   98.2/68 C     100.0%          6000 / 5800 RPM
117.6 s   emergency   96.8/72 C     100.0%          6000 / 5800 RPM
```

At full fan speed, CPU remaining around 95–97 C reflects the machine's limit
under an unusually heavy synthetic load, not a failure to command fans.

A GPU-only run advanced the GPU target from level 19 to 28 at 74 C. CPU still
became the final controller because CUDA host overhead and shared cooling
raised it to 87.5 C. This exposed a brief Auto-return race while raw CPU was hot
but EWMA was cool; cleanup now requires both temperatures below release.

A power-instrumented repeat measured 174.6 W maximum dGPU draw, with 111
samples at or above 170 W and 119 at or above 160 W. `power.limit` was not
reported, so only actual draw is claimed. GPU peaked at 74 C. CPU reached
93.8 C through shared heat/host overhead, correctly invoking 6,000/6,000 RPM.

Across these tests, measurable RPM began about three seconds after the first
manual request and maximum speed could take roughly 20 seconds from pre-spin.
A temperature-only controller cannot eliminate an instantaneous synthetic
transient, but it removes the sustained firmware-Auto ceiling.

## Proposed OmenCore feature

Add an opt-in automatic controller with this control path:

1. Probe board identity, `0x2c` capabilities, and `0x2f`; reject unknown
   formats by default.
2. Sample CPU, GPU, and a proven chassis/IR sensor once per second.
3. Apply configurable asymmetric smoothing and per-sensor rise/fall curves.
4. Select the highest request and map physical fans through `0x2f`.
5. Write only changed levels at a conservative cadence; allow immediate rises.
6. Enable only for selected profiles and restore Auto on exit, profile change,
   suspend, service failure, reboot, or shutdown.

Daemon-enforced safety invariants should include strict curve validation,
model allowlisting, a raw critical-temperature override, sensor-loss handling,
a watchdog/fail-open path, rate limiting, and clear telemetry. Curve files must
not disable them, and userspace control does not replace hardware throttling or
shutdown.

The same backend can support custom curves through a small privileged daemon
and unprivileged CLI/TUI. Human-readable configuration should support
per-profile CPU/GPU/IR curves, import/export, live raw/filtered temperatures,
the winning curve, mapped levels/RPM, and offline CSV replay. Invalid changes
must be rejected atomically while the last known-good configuration remains
active. The standalone prototype already supports separate curves and the
factory preset in TOML; it is evidence, not proposed OmenCore code.

## Applicability beyond `8D87`

Linux 7.1 includes the same implementation for these Victus/OMEN-family IDs:

```text
8902  8A44  8A4D  8BAB  8BBE  8BC2  8BCA  8BCD  8BD4
8BD5  8C76  8C77  8C78  8C99  8C9C  8D41  8D87
```

This suggests broader applicability, not identical defects or mappings.
Unknown systems should start in read-only onboarding that records DMI/kernel,
hwmon channels/modes, `0x2c`, `0x2f`, and a bounded actuator/Auto-restore test.
Writes should require an explicit supported-device entry or successful
validation; board ID alone is insufficient.

Kernel references:

- Linux 7.1 `hp-wmi` implementation and quirks:
  <https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v7.1/drivers/platform/x86/hp/hp-wmi.c#L2248-L2410>
- Current upstream PWM implementation:
  <https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/platform/x86/hp/hp-wmi.c#L2594-L2654>

## Remaining questions

- What `0x2f` variants exist on other supported generations?
- Can OmenCore already expose the full per-fan mapping, or is a backend API
  needed?
- Should curves be profile-indexed or run only in Performance?
- Does firmware require periodic refresh when the requested level is unchanged?
- What is the strongest practical recovery path for `SIGKILL` or a crash?
- Actuator/restoration behavior and mappings remain unvalidated outside `8D87`.

Everything central to this report is directly confirmed on `8D87`: active
Performance power limits, the firmware-Auto ceiling, Gaming Hub's userspace
algorithm and selected factory resource, WMI commands/payloads, exact `0x2f`,
intermediate and maximum actuation, factory-curve behavior, CPU/GPU/combined
loads, NVIDIA power draw, profile persistence, and clean Auto restoration.

body:
# Linux: OMEN MAX 16-ak0xxx (8D87) per-key RGB confirmed — Darfon 0D62:54BF / HID interface 3

## System

- **Laptop:** HP OMEN MAX Gaming Laptop 16-ak0xxx
- **Board/Product ID:** `8D87`
- **Linux:** Omarchy 4.0.1 / Arch Linux
- **Kernel:** `7.1.9-arch1-2`
- **OmenCore:** `4.2.0`

## Keyboard hardware

The internal keyboard enumerates as:

```text
idVendor  0x0d62 Darfon Electronics Corp.
idProduct 0x54bf HP Gaming Keyboard II
```

It exposes five HID interfaces:

```text
hidraw1 -> USB interface 0
hidraw2 -> USB interface 1
hidraw3 -> USB interface 2
hidraw4 -> USB interface 3
hidraw5 -> USB interface 4
```

All interfaces are currently handled by `hid-generic`.

## Current OmenCore behavior

Running:

```bash
sudo ./omencore-cli keyboard --brightness 30 --verbose
```

returns:

```text
⚠ Keyboard brightness unsupported: Brightness sysfs path not found: /sys/class/leds/hp::kbd_backlight/brightness
```

There is no:

```text
/sys/class/leds/hp::kbd_backlight
```

on this system.

I also couldn't find an HP keyboard RGB interface exposed through sysfs such as:

```text
hp::kbd_backlight
hp_omen::kbd_backlight
rgb_zones
zone_colors
keyboardleds
```

So the keyboard RGB controller on this model does not appear to be exposed through the HP WMI/sysfs LED interface currently expected by OmenCore.

## HID per-key RGB confirmation

I tested the userspace HID implementation from `arfelious/omen-rgb-linux`.

RGB control works correctly through:

```text
/dev/hidraw4
```

which corresponds to **USB HID interface 3** of:

```text
VID:PID 0D62:54BF
HP Gaming Keyboard II
```

### Confirmed working

- [x] Full-keyboard static RGB color
- [x] Per-key RGB control
- [x] Individual `Esc` key set to red
- [x] Individual `W`, `A`, `S`, `D` keys set to green

For example, I successfully tested:

```bash
python scripts/omen_cli.py static '#202020'
python scripts/omen_cli.py set-key esc '#ff0000'

python scripts/omen_cli.py set-key w '#00ff00'
python scripts/omen_cli.py set-key a '#00ff00'
python scripts/omen_cli.py set-key s '#00ff00'
python scripts/omen_cli.py set-key d '#00ff00'
```

The result was correct: the keyboard was set to the base color, `Esc` was independently red, and `W/A/S/D` were independently green.

## Confirmed hardware mapping

For the **OMEN MAX 16-ak0xxx / board 8D87**:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Keyboard | HP Gaming Keyboard II |
| Vendor | Darfon Electronics Corp. |
| VID | `0D62` |
| PID | `54BF` |
| RGB HID interface | **3** |
| Device during this boot | `/dev/hidraw4` |
| Global/static RGB | ✅ Confirmed |
| Per-key RGB | ✅ Confirmed |
| OmenCore sysfs brightness path | ❌ Not available |

Obviously `/dev/hidrawN` should not be considered stable across boots. The important identifiers appear to be:

```text
VID:PID = 0D62:54BF
HID interface = 3
```

## Conclusion

This appears to confirm the HID per-key RGB hardware mapping for the `8D87` OMEN MAX platform.

The keyboard itself and its per-key RGB controller work correctly under Linux using direct userspace HID communication.

The current issue with OmenCore seems to be backend/device discovery: OmenCore attempts to use the `hp::kbd_backlight` sysfs interface, while this keyboard's RGB controller is accessible through USB HID interface 3 instead.

I'm happy to provide additional information such as:

- `lsusb -v`
- HID report descriptors
- `/sys/class/hidraw` topology
- OmenCore `diagnose` output
- raw HID device information

I can also test a patch, branch, or development build on the actual `8D87` hardware if that would be useful.

### With OmenCore

- **CPU:** ~50 W
- **GPU:** ~75 W

Previously, this laptop was able to reach approximately:

- **CPU:** ~60 W
- **GPU:** ~115–120 W

under the same type of combined CPU + GPU load.

When Performance mode is applied, OmenCore reports:

`Power limits applied: CPU=95W, GPU=140W`

followed by:

`Performance mode 'Performance' applied successfully`

Despite this, the observed GPU power can be substantially below what I previously saw on this machine.

I am still testing whether this is directly related to the GPU Power Boost state described below.

---

## 2. Saved GPU Power Boost = Maximum, but Hardware Can Start at Minimum

This may be related to the reduced GPU wattage.

OmenCore restores the saved configuration as:

`Restored last GPU Power Boost level from config: Maximum`

but hardware detection can subsequently report:

`GPU Power Boost available via WMI BIOS. Detected: Minimum, User pref: Maximum`

OmenCore then does not automatically restore the requested state because startup restore is intentionally blocked on this model:

`Startup performance restore is disabled - skipping automatic GPU Power Boost reapply`

Therefore, it appears possible for the saved preference/UI to indicate **Maximum** while the actual firmware/hardware state is still **Minimum** after startup.

When I manually apply Maximum, the WMI operation appears to work correctly:

`Sending GPU power command: Level=Maximum, CustomTgp=1, PPAB=1, DState=1`

followed by:

`GPU power readback attempt 1: CustomTgp=True, PPAB=1, DState=1`

and:

`✓ GPU power set and verified: Maximum`

`✓ GPU Power Boost set to: Maximum via WMI BIOS`

This seems important because a user could believe Maximum is active based on the saved preference while the actual hardware remains at Minimum until Maximum is manually reapplied.

---

## 3. Possible NVAPI Power-Limit Capability/UI Inconsistency

The OmenCore UI displays:

`Maximum (Custom TGP + Dynamic Boost +15W) (NVAPI power limits available)`

The UI also displays:

`BOOST ACTIVE`

and:

`Extra Power +15W`

However, the application log reports:

`NVAPI: NVAPI returned no writable power policy entries`

and later:

`GPU OC initialized: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU, Supports OC: True, Supports Power Limit: False`

The working Maximum GPU Power Boost operation appears to be through HP WMI BIOS instead:

`✓ GPU Power Boost set to: Maximum via WMI BIOS`

So the UI appears to report that NVAPI power limits are available even though the backend reports that there are no writable NVAPI power-policy entries.

I'm not sure whether this is only a UI/capability-detection issue or whether it also affects TGP behavior.

---

## 4. Extended GPU Power Boost Readback Failure / Possible False Success

I also found a failure when using an Extended GPU Power Boost level:

`GPU power command was accepted but readback did not match requested level Extended3`

However, OmenCore subsequently reports:

`✓ GPU Power Boost set to: Extended via EC (experimental)`

This appears potentially misleading because the requested Extended state did not pass readback verification, but a success message is still displayed/logged afterwards.

On this 8A44 system, **Maximum through WMI appears to verify correctly**, while the Extended/experimental state does not.

---

## 5. CPU Temperature Source Problems / Fallback Timeouts

The HP WMI CPU temperature appears inaccurate on this laptop.

OmenCore correctly detects this and switches to the LibreHardwareMonitor worker. For example:

`WMI/ACPI reading looked invalid (51.0°C), using LibreHardwareMonitor (69.6°C)`

This fallback generally works, but I have also seen:

`CPU temp fallback timed out after 500ms`

and later:

`CPU temperature appears frozen at 63.1°C for 21 readings`

OmenCore's recovery/fallback logic appears to prevent an immediate failure, but CPU temperature telemetry does not appear completely reliable on this model.

---

## 6. GPU Temperature Can Also Be Detected as Frozen

Diagnostics also recorded:

`GPU temperature appears frozen at 51.0°C for 21 readings (load=47%, load swing during hold=42%)`

The GPU load changed considerably during this period while the reported GPU temperature remained fixed at 51°C.

This may indicate another telemetry/source issue worth checking on 8A44.

---

## 7. Fan RPM Readback Fails, but Fan Level/Control Works

During runtime capability probing OmenCore reports:

`✗ Fan RPM readback returned null`

However:

- Fan level readback works
- Fan level writes work
- Custom fan curves work
- WMI fan control works
- Extreme fan preset works
- Fan commands verify successfully

For example:

`✓ Fan level readback works: Fan1=33, Fan2=30`

and later:

`✓ Fan levels set: CPU=47, GPU=47`

`✓ Fan speed set to 87% (Level: 47)`

So this appears specifically related to RPM readback rather than fan control itself.

---

## 8. Features I Can Confirm Are Working on Real 8A44 Hardware

Since this model is currently marked as unverified, I can confirm the following from actual use:

- HP WMI BIOS interface works
- Two fans are detected
- WMI BIOS fan control works
- Fan level readback works
- Custom fan curves work
- Performance mode commands work
- Default / Performance / Cool modes are detected
- MUX switch is detected
- Discrete GPU Only mode detection works
- RTX 3070 Ti is correctly detected through NVAPI
- GPU Power Boost Maximum can be applied and verified through WMI BIOS
- CPU and GPU monitoring generally work, with the telemetry issues described above
- 4-zone keyboard RGB works
- WMI BIOS ColorTable backend works
- Keyboard color writes pass readback verification
- PawnIO EC access works
- Secure Boot works with the PawnIO backend

CPU undervolting is correctly hidden/disabled for this model by the capability database.

---

## Expected Behavior

1. If GPU Power Boost is shown as Maximum/active, the actual hardware state should also be Maximum, or the UI should clearly indicate that the saved preference has not been applied.

2. The UI should not report `NVAPI power limits available` if NVAPI reports no writable power policy.

3. A failed Extended GPU Power Boost readback should not subsequently be reported as successfully applied without clearly indicating that verification failed.

4. CPU/GPU temperature telemetry should recover reliably without prolonged frozen values.

5. If supported by the hardware interface, fan RPM readback should work on 8A44.

6. Performance mode should provide the expected CPU/GPU power behavior for this model.

---

## Reduced Power Test

| Configuration | CPU Power | GPU Power |
|---|---:|---:|
| Previous behavior | ~60 W | ~115–120 W |
| OmenCore observed behavior | ~50 W | ~75 W |

I will also retest after rebooting and explicitly pressing **Apply** on GPU Power Boost → Maximum rather than relying on the saved Maximum preference.

If manually applying Maximum restores the previous ~115–120 W GPU behavior, that would suggest the startup GPU Power Boost state mismatch is responsible.

If the GPU remains around ~75 W even after Maximum is manually applied and successfully verified, then there may be an additional Performance/TGP configuration issue for Product ID 8A44.

---

## Attachments

I am attaching:

- Full OmenCore v4.1.0 diagnostics ZIP
- Screenshot showing Performance mode / Extreme fan mode / Maximum GPU Power Boost
- Stress-test screenshots/results if required

I can perform additional WMI, fan, GPU power, performance-mode, RGB or telemetry tests on the physical 8A44 system if useful for verifying the model profile.

body: ## Environment - Model: OMEN MAX Gaming Laptop 16-ah0xxx - Board ID: 8D41 - OS: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon) - Kernel: 7.0.0-27-generic - OmenCore version: 3.3.0 (.NET 8.0.25 runtime) - Secure Boot: disabled ## Summary The internal keyboard has RGB backlighting currently stuck in a factory-default rainbow-cycle animation. No Linux tool currently available (hp-rgb-lighting driver via OmenCommandCenterforLinux, OmenCore) can change it, and neither can HP's own official Windows software (OMEN Light Studio) once tested against this exact hardware identity. Root cause appears to be that this board's keyboard RGB is physically controlled through a separate USB HID controller (Darfon), not through the ACPI/WMI zone mechanism that existing tools use for the chassis light bar. ## Keyboard controller identity Internal keyboard enumerates as an independent USB HID device, isolated on its own port (confirmed via `lsusb -t`, no shared hub with touchpad/webcam): Bus 003 Device 004: ID 0d62:54bf Darfon Electronics Corp. HP Gaming Keyboard II |__ Port 009: Dev 004, If 0-4, Class=Human Interface Device, Driver=usbhid, 12M 5 HID interfaces confirmed via /sys/class/hidraw (hidraw2-hidraw6), e.g.: HID_ID=0003:00000D62:000054BF HID_NAME=HP HP Gaming Keyboard II HID_PHYS=usb-0000:80:14.0-9/input{0..4} MODALIAS=hid:b0003g0001v00000D62p000054BF dmesg at boot: hp_rgb_lighting: loading out-of-tree module taints kernel. hp_rgb_lighting: module verification failed: signature and/or required key missing - tainting kernel hp_rgb_lighting: hp-rgb-lighting: init starting... hp_rgb_lighting: hp-rgb-lighting: WMI GUID found OK hp_rgb_lighting: hp-rgb-lighting: platform device registered OK hp_rgb_lighting: HP Omen/Victus RGB companion driver loaded hp_wmi: Registered as platform profile handler No LED class device exposed for it — `/sys/class/leds/` only shows capslock/numlock/scrolllock (input3, input36, input47) and network LEDs, nothing keyboard-RGB related. ## hp-rgb-lighting sysfs interface (via OmenCommandCenterforLinux v1.6.3) For board 8D41, the installer explicitly overrides the stock driver: [WARN] Board 8D41 detected — forcing custom hp-wmi install path on kernel 7.0.0-27-generic. Resulting sysfs tree: /sys/devices/platform/hp-rgb-lighting/{brightness,win_lock,zone0..zone7} ### zone0-zone3: front light bar — works correctly Verified by writing each zone individually; color change is visually confirmed on the physical light bar and persists on read-back. ### zone4-zone7: keyboard — accepted by the driver but never reaches hardware Read-back behavior is inconsistent depending on timing, which is itself informative: - **Immediate read-back** (`cat` right after `echo ... | tee zoneN`, no delay): returns `000000` — appears as if the write was dropped entirely. - **Read-back after ~0.3s delay**: returns the written value correctly (confirmed via an automated test script that writes `FF00FF` to all 8 zones and reads back after a short sleep — see full output below). So the sysfs attribute *does* retain the written value internally (given a brief delay), for zone4-7 as well as zone0-3. However, **the physical keyboard never changes color** in either case — only the front light bar responds. This was re-confirmed with `hpm-rgb`/`hpm-*` systemd services both running and fully stopped (`systemctl stop hpm-rgb ...`), ruling out the animation engine as the cause of anything — same result regardless of service state. This suggests the driver accepts the value into some internal/software state for zone4-7, but the write pipeline never reaches the actual keyboard controller — i.e. these zones may be a generic 8-zone template inherited from other OMEN models, with only zone0-3 (light bar) wired to a real register on this board. Full zone test output (script-based, FF00FF test value, 0.3s delay before read): --- zone0 --- Valor original: FFFF00 → FF00FF (bar changes, confirmed visually) --- zone1 --- Valor original: FFFF00 → FF00FF (bar changes, confirmed visually) --- zone2 --- Valor original: FFFF00 → FF00FF (bar changes, confirmed visually) --- zone3 --- Valor original: FFFF00 → FF00FF (bar changes, confirmed visually) --- zone4 --- Valor original: 000000 → FF00FF (keyboard unchanged, still rainbow-cycling) --- zone5 --- Valor original: 000000 → FF00FF (keyboard unchanged, still rainbow-cycling) --- zone6 --- Valor original: 000000 → FF00FF (keyboard unchanged, still rainbow-cycling) --- zone7 --- Valor original: 000000 → FF00FF (keyboard unchanged, still rainbow-cycling) ## OmenCore keyboard command — fails outright $ sudo ./omencore-cli diagnose ⚠ Model 'OMEN MAX Gaming Laptop 16-ah0xxx' (board '8D41') detected - direct EC register access disabled (different register layout or firmware watchdog behavior). Using safe interface: hp-wmi-hwmon ... EC Safety: ⚠ Blocked (new model) KEYBOARD LIGHTING: HP WMI: ✓ Available Despite reporting keyboard lighting as "available": $ sudo ./omencore-cli keyboard --color 00FFFF --zone 0 --verbose ✗ Failed to set keyboard color $ sudo ./omencore-cli keyboard --color 00FFFF --verbose ✗ Failed to set keyboard color Same generic failure with and without `--zone`, no additional detail despite `--verbose`, no application log file found anywhere (`~/.local/share`, `/var/log`, `/tmp` all checked — only a dotnet-suggest sentinel file exists). `config --show` confirms no hidden override key exists for the EC safety block (only `fan.*`, `perf.mode`, `keyboard.color`, `keyboard.brightness`, `startup.apply`). I deliberately did not attempt to bypass the EC safety gate, given the project's own conservative-identity policy for boards with an unmapped register layout. ## Also tested: HP's own official software (Windows, virtualized) No native Windows dual-boot available on this machine, so the Darfon device was passed through to a VirtualBox Windows 11 VM (USB filter by vendor/ product ID; `lsusb -t` confirms the device sits on its own port, safe to pass through). - Windows Device Manager sees it only as generic "Dispositivo de teclado HID" (x2) + standard PS/2 keyboard — no HP-branded driver loads. - OMEN Light Studio 1.0.68.0 (2026-05-18 — latest per in-app changelog, which only mentions Wave/Radial flicker fixes, no new device support) initially failed with: "Dispositivos conectados no compatibles con OMEN Light Studio." - Root cause: VirtualBox reports genuine VM identity by default (`wmic csproduct get vendor,name` → `innotek GmbH` / `VirtualBox`), and Light Studio appears to gate device support on system DMI identity, not just the USB device ID. - Worked around via EFI DMI spoofing (VM uses EFI firmware — the legacy `pcbios/0/Config` path fails with `VERR_CFGM_VALUE_NOT_FOUND` on BootDevice0 for EFI VMs; the `efi/0/Config` path must be used instead): VBoxManage setextradata "Windows 11" "VBoxInternal/Devices/efi/0/Config/DmiSystemVendor" "HP" VBoxManage setextradata "Windows 11" "VBoxInternal/Devices/efi/0/Config/DmiSystemProduct" "OMEN MAX Gaming Laptop 16-ah0xxx" VBoxManage setextradata "Windows 11" "VBoxInternal/Devices/efi/0/Config/DmiSystemVersion" "1.0" VBoxManage setextradata "Windows 11" "VBoxInternal/Devices/efi/0/Config/DmiBoardVendor" "HP" VBoxManage setextradata "Windows 11" "VBoxInternal/Devices/efi/0/Config/DmiBoardProduct" "8D41" VBoxManage setextradata "Windows 11" "VBoxInternal/Devices/efi/0/Config/DmiBIOSVendor" "HP" - After spoofing, Light Studio correctly rendered the exact chassis silhouette (light bar + full keyboard incl. numpad + touchpad) and showed a pre-existing "Wave" effect layer — but still reported: "Lamentablemente, este dispositivo no es compatible con OMEN Light Studio," this time specifically over the keyboard/HID region rather than the whole chassis. This suggests Light Studio's device compatibility check has at least two gates: (1) system DMI identity [bypassed via spoof], and (2) a vendor/ product (and possibly firmware-version) whitelist for the actual HID keyboard controller, which does not yet include this Darfon unit — i.e. even HP's own current shipping software doesn't recognize this exact keyboard controller. Not a Linux-specific gap. ## Hypothesis The keyboard RGB on this board is driven via HID feature reports sent directly to the Darfon 0d62:54bf controller (5 report interfaces suggest distinct usage pages for keyboard input, RGB control, consumer control, etc.), independent of the hp-wmi ACPI zone mechanism that correctly drives the chassis light bar. The 8 zones exposed by hp-rgb-lighting for this board are likely a generic template (front-bar zones 0-3 real and wired; keyboard zones 4-7 accepted into an internal/software state but never flushed to the real controller). ## Reference: related OmenCore tracking Noted in OmenCore's own release tracking for board 8D41 (OMEN MAX 16 ah0500na): RGB light-bar-vs-keyboard routing still needs a session log — this report is intended to serve as exactly that. ## What I can help with going forward - USB HID report captures via usbhid-dump or Wireshark+usbmon while toggling effects in Light Studio inside the VM (device passed through), if that would help reverse-engineer the feature report format. - Any additional diagnostic exports OmenCore's Report Model flow requests. - Testing patches/branches against this exact board+controller combination. Let me know what would be most useful to move this forward.

title: perf(ui): reduce unnecessary UI-thread work
body:
This PR reduces unnecessary UI-thread work identified while investigating Issue #133.

## Summary
This PR reduces unnecessary UI‑thread work while preserving existing behavior. It addresses performance concerns raised in GitHub issue #133 by tightening log handling, pausing the dashboard uptime timer when inactive, and avoiding redundant tray‑icon refreshes.

## Changes
- **Log buffering** – Introduced a `StringBuilder` in `MainViewModel` and rebuilt the buffer only when the log line queue exceeds the UI limit.
- **Dashboard uptime timer** – Timer start is now deferred; `SetUptimeTimerEnabled` starts the timer when telemetry projection is enabled and stops it when disabled.
- **Tray icon caching** – Added cached fields for all displayed metrics, implemented early‑return when values are unchanged, and updated caches after a UI refresh.
- **Allocation reduction** – Fewer string allocations and dispatcher posts across the UI.
- **Code cleanup** – Removed a duplicate cache‑update block in `TrayIconService`.

## Behavior
No functional changes are intended. All UI elements continue to display the same information; only the amount of work performed on the UI thread is reduced.

## Testing
- `dotnet build OmenCore.sln` succeeds with 0 warnings and 0 errors.
- All existing unit tests (`OmenCoreApp.Tests`) pass.
- Manual verification confirms:
  - Log view updates correctly after appending and after buffer reload.
  - Dashboard uptime counter updates only when the dashboard is visible.
  - Tray tooltip, menu, and badge updates occur only when a displayed value actually changes.

## Expected Impact
- Lower CPU usage on the UI thread during idle periods.
- Fewer allocations and garbage‑collection pressure.
- Reduced dispatcher activity leading to smoother UI responsiveness, especially when the app is monitoring continuously.

Related to #133

title: Support / TGP fix for HP OMEN Max 16-ah0xxx / RTX 5080, baseboard 8D41
body:
**Describe the issue**

On the HP OMEN Max 16-ah0xxx (baseboard 8D41) with an RTX 5080, the GPU TGP is permanently capped at 80W on Linux. The GPU supports up to 175W and reaches it correctly on Windows with OMEN Gaming Hub.

nvidia-powerd starts and connects over DBus but immediately logs:

    ERROR! Client (presumably SBIOS) has requested to disable Dynamic Boost DC controller

After that it goes idle. Requested Power Limit stays N/A and the GPU never moves off 80W regardless of load or platform profile.

nvidia-smi -pl is blocked by design on Blackwell laptop GPUs -- nvidia-powerd is the only valid path to raise TGP.

**Root cause**

After going through hp-wmi.c, board 8D41 is present in victus_s_thermal_profile_boards[] but mapped to omen_v1_no_ec_thermal_params, which was added as a crash-prevention placeholder (ec_tp_offset = HP_NO_THERMAL_PROFILE_OFFSET). This entry skips the GPU TGP unlock path entirely.

On Windows, OMEN Gaming Hub sends two WMI commands on performance mode:

  1. HPWMI_SET_PERFORMANCE_MODE (0x1A) with thermal profile 0x31 -- sent by Linux driver
  2. HPWMI_SET_GPU_THERMAL_MODES_QUERY (0x22) with ctgp_enable=1, ppab_enable=1 -- NOT sent for 8D41

Without command 2 the BIOS never raises the NvPCF power budget, nvidia-powerd receives the disable signal, and TGP stays at 80W.

I have filed a bug upstream at platform-driver-x86@vger.kernel.org with an ACPI dump and a suggested fix.

**Hardware**

    Laptop  : HP OMEN Max Gaming Laptop 16-ah0xxx
    Board   : 8D41
    BIOS    : F.06
    GPU     : NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 Laptop GPU
    Driver  : 595.71.05
    Kernel  : 7.0.3-1-cachyos
    OS      : CachyOS (Arch-based)

**What I have tried**

- nvidia-powerd enabled and running -- connects but goes idle immediately
- powerprofilesctl set performance -- thermal profile set but no GPU unlock
- OmenCore -- sets performance mode, EC access disabled for 8D41, still 80W
- nvidia-smi -pl 175 -- blocked by design
- driver 595.71.05 (latest) -- no change

**References**

  NVIDIA Developer Forums (same issue, RTX 5070 Ti variant):
  https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/hp-omen-max-16-rtx-5070-ti-laptop-gpu-power-locked-at-80w-on-linux-ubuntu-24-04-3-lts/351924

  Related OmenCore thread (8D41 EC access confirmed disabled):
  https://github.com/theantipopau/omencore/issues/91

Happy to test patches or provide any further output.
